ai-at-work.title: Anthropic to pay Akamai $11.6 billion over seven years in cloud deal
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic has committed $11.6 billion over seven years to Akamai's cloud infrastructure, a bet on CPUs that could grow to about $20 billion, and in an unusual arrangement, Akamai is giving Anthropic a
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic just locked in an $11.6 billion cloud infrastructure deal with Akamai over seven years, with potential equity upside for the AI company if spending hits $20 billion. This matters because it signals where serious compute power is flowing and shows that infrastructure providers are now willing to bet equity on their biggest customers, which changes the economics of how enterprises negotiate cloud deals going forward. Turns out the real AI gold rush isn't building the models, it's owning the pipes that run them.

ai-at-work.title: Mark Wahlberg is coming to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, and he wants to talk about your work, not his
ai-at-work.excerpt: Mark Wahlberg joins Bruce K. Lee at Disrupt to discuss investing, entrepreneurship, healthcare, wellness, and building businesses.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Mark Wahlberg is headlining TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 to talk about investing, entrepreneurship, and business building alongside Bruce K. Lee. This matters because when celebrities start showing up at tech conferences talking about workplace culture and business strategy, it signals that digital transformation and workplace innovation have officially moved beyond the IT department into mainstream business conversation. Look, if Marky Mark can get people interested in wellness and entrepreneurship at a tech conference, maybe there's hope that executives will actually listen to their workplace strategists for once.

ai-at-work.title: Ahead of US IPO, British AI neocloud Nscale secures $3.36B in convertible financing
ai-at-work.excerpt: The funding, which comes from Third Point, Nvidia, and others, will fuel the company's massive AI data center buildout.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: British AI infrastructure company Nscale just locked down $3.36 billion in convertible financing from heavy hitters like Third Point and Nvidia to build out massive data centers ahead of going public in the US. This matters to digital workplace pros because AI infrastructure investments at this scale signal that generative AI tooling for enterprise work is moving from "interesting pilot" to "mission critical infrastructure," which means your organization's AI strategy better be more than a chatbot experiment. Honestly, watching investors throw this much money at data centers reminds me that while everyone's arguing about AI governance policies, the real game is being played by whoever controls the compute underneath it all.

ai-at-work.title: Meta’s Muse just stole the AI spotlight from OpenAI and Anthropic
ai-at-work.excerpt: When AI leaders at OpenAI and Anthropic started talking about “pacing the frontier,” maybe someone should have asked: what pace? Now it’s turned into model drop week for both companies as Anthropic ro
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent that's apparently outperforming ChatGPT in early comparisons, while OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a rapid-fire model release cycle trying to keep up. For digital workplace folks, this matters because your AI tool choices are about to get a lot messier, and vendors will be claiming superiority based on benchmarks that shift faster than your CEO's priorities. The real joke here is that organizations are still trying to figure out how to use the last generation of AI while three companies are already racing toward the next one like it's Black Friday at Best Buy.

tools-tech.title: Your LG TV is constantly collecting your data – here’s how to stop it
tools-tech.excerpt: Factory resetting your LG TV is the only way to remove certain data logs from its hardware.
tools-tech.dwp_take: LG TVs are collecting user data and storing it in ways that persist even after you try to delete it, requiring a full factory reset to actually remove the logs. This matters to digital workplace pros because it's a stark reminder that the "smart" devices employees bring into hybrid work setups are basically data collection machines, and IT departments need to have real conversations about what happens when personal devices end up on corporate networks. Turns out your TV knows more about your viewing habits than your company knows about its own data governance, which is either hilarious or terrifying depending on your caffeine intake.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft’s new Copilot app puts everything in one place – but the price is ‘evolving’
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft says Copilot has gotten ‘actually really good.’ The new app has AI agents and can write code. So how much is all this going to cost?
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft bundled Copilot into a single app with AI agents and coding capabilities, but they're being deliberately vague about pricing, calling it "evolving." This matters because most organizations are still struggling to figure out their existing AI spend, and Microsoft's pricing fog just made it harder to budget for enterprise deployments. After three decades, I've learned that when a vendor says pricing is "evolving," what they really mean is "we'll charge whatever we can get away with once you're locked in."

tools-tech.title: OpenAI wants you to use AI — but not to train its AI
tools-tech.excerpt: Here’s an interesting concept: an AI company that fires people for using AI. It sounds like a strange way to run a company but there’s a real reason behind it. OpenAI has been hiring contractors who h
tools-tech.dwp_take: OpenAI discovered contractors hired to manually review ChatGPT prompts were using AI tools to do the work, defeating the purpose of having humans in the loop for quality control. This matters because it highlights a real tension in AI workflows: when you make AI tools too good and accessible, even people paid to do human-level work will automate themselves out of a job. The irony is delicious, but it also exposes why AI augmentation strategies fail when companies don't think through actual human behavior and incentive structures.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft’s new Copilot ‘super app’ unifies chat, code, agents
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft’s Copilot “super app” has arrived, two months after CEO Satya Nadella confirmed it was in development. It combines conversational Chat, the autonomous Cowork agent, a redesigned coding envir
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft bundled its AI chat, coding, agent, and automation tools into one unified Copilot interface instead of keeping them scattered across different applications. This matters because it reduces tool sprawl and could actually make AI features discoverable for workers who currently ignore half the stuff their company pays for. Whether this "super app" approach genuinely improves workflow or just creates a new dumping ground for features nobody asked for remains to be seen.

digital-culture.title: The tradwife debate is really about control
digital-culture.excerpt: The tradwife has entered the conversation. Instagram showcases her baking bread, doing laundry, and extolling the virtues of domestic bliss—a counterpoint to the girlboss who is always working, and al
digital-culture.dwp_take: A cultural debate about "tradwives" versus "girlbosses" is playing out on social media as people argue over whether domestic life or career ambition represents the better choice for women. This matters to digital workplace folks because it reflects real tension in how we design work, support flexibility, and message company culture to employees who have vastly different life priorities. The truth is neither extreme works for most people, and any organization still pushing the "always on, always grinding" narrative is just asking for burnout and turnover.

digital-culture.title: This is what your highest performers really want
digital-culture.excerpt: At a moment when employers are sinking billions of dollars into AI adoption, workforce development has become less of a priority. Training budgets have contracted, forcing companies to make tough choi
digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are cutting training budgets while pouring money into AI, which means they're choosing which employees get development support instead of investing across the board. This matters because your best people will leave if they feel ignored, and ironically, they're usually the ones most likely to find opportunities elsewhere. Here's the thing: starving your high performers of growth while building expensive AI systems is like buying a Ferrari and forgetting to put gas in it.

digital-culture.title: Workers are faking their interest in AI to satisfy bosses, report shows
digital-culture.excerpt: Corporate leaders are putting tremendous pressure on workers to incorporate artificial intelligence into their workflow—often without a clear understanding of its capabilities or impact. As a result,
digital-culture.dwp_take: Workers are pretending to use AI tools and exaggerating their skills with them because management is pushing adoption without any real strategy or business case. This matters because it signals a breakdown in trust between leadership and workers, and it means your organization has zero visibility into actual AI adoption and value. Here's the thing: when bosses mandate solutions looking for problems instead of solving actual problems, people will absolutely game the metrics, and you'll end up with a false sense of progress while your real work doesn't improve one bit.

digital-culture.title: How solopreneurs can use AI as a behind-the-scenes assistant
digital-culture.excerpt: Every week, as a solo business owner, I have an entire list of tasks that need to get done on top of my client work. If they don’t get done by Friday, they’re staring at me when I begin work again the
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece about solo entrepreneurs using AI to handle repetitive admin work so they can focus on billable client time. This matters to digital workplace folks because it's the exact same tension that plagues knowledge workers everywhere: how do you carve out space for actual thinking when the busywork piles up. The real lesson isn't "buy more AI tools" but rather that every organization needs to stop treating administrative overhead like some character-building exercise and start treating it as the productivity thief it actually is.

industry-news.title: Microsoft Unveils Surface Pro 12-Inch and Laptop 13-Inch With Snapdragon X2 Plus
industry-news.excerpt: Microsoft’s Surface Pro 12-inch and Laptop 13-inch add Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. Compare pricing, battery life, AI features, and key checks for IT buyers. The post Microsoft Unveils Surface Pro 12-Inc
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft dropped new Surface Pro and Laptop models with Snapdragon X2 Plus chips, which means better battery life and on-device AI capabilities for mobile workers. This matters because IT teams need to understand whether these ARM-based processors actually work with your existing software stack and whether the AI features justify the upgrade costs. Here's the thing though: every new processor generation gets marketed as a game changer, but I've seen plenty of "revolutionary" devices end up in desk drawers because they broke something important or cost way too much for marginal gains.

industry-news.title: NVIDIA Releases Open Viral Protein Dataset and BioNeMo Pipeline
industry-news.excerpt: NVIDIA released AI-predicted protein structures for more than 2,800 viruses and an open BioNeMo pipeline to help researchers prepare for future outbreaks. The post NVIDIA Releases Open Viral Protein D
industry-news.dwp_take: NVIDIA just dropped protein structures for thousands of viruses and an open-source pipeline called BioNeMo to help researchers prep for the next outbreak. This matters because biotech companies and research teams need accessible AI tools to work faster, and giving away datasets accelerates innovation instead of hoarding it behind paywalls like some companies do. Honestly, when a chipmaker starts solving public health problems better than most governments, you know we're living in weird times, but I'll take it.

industry-news.title: Google, OpenAI, Anthropic Reportedly Plan AI Safety Standards Body
industry-news.excerpt: Google, OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly plan an AI safety standards body. See what the proposed testing and audits could mean for enterprise IT buyers. The post Google, OpenAI, Anthropic Reportedly Pl
industry-news.dwp_take: Three major AI players want to create their own standards body for AI safety, which sounds noble until you realize they're basically writing their own report cards. This matters because enterprises are already scrambling to figure out what's safe to deploy in their digital workplaces, and competing safety frameworks from vendors create confusion rather than clarity. You've got to love the irony: companies racing to dominate the AI market are now promising to police themselves, which historically works about as well as a fox guarding the henhouse.

industry-news.title: Google May Remove the Android Feature That Tells You to Look Up
industry-news.excerpt: Google appears to be preparing to retire Android’s Heads Up feature, a Digital Wellbeing tool that warns users when they walk while using their phones. The post Google May Remove the Android Feature T
industry-news.dwp_take: Google is reportedly killing off Android's Heads Up feature, which warned users when they were walking while staring at their phones. This matters because digital workplace professionals spend half their day selling us on "digital wellbeing" tools while designing apps specifically engineered to be addictive, so losing even a small safety guardrail feels like the house of cards it always was. I guess Google figured if people want to walk into fountains while scrolling Slack, that's their right to choose.
